bp: This paper is about a practical measurement problem: decentralized finance systems produce long public histories of user actions, but the research community still needs a fair way to test whether methods can understand those histories over time. The concrete system is Aave v3, a Web3 lending protocol where transactions are recorded as time-stamped events. A user may arrive, borrow, repay, supply assets, stop returning, or move into another behavior state. Those changes matter because web platforms, financial systems, and risk tools all need to know not only what users did once, but how their behavior evolves. The paper presents the FinSurvival Challenge 2025 as a benchmark, meaning a shared task setup that lets different teams compare answers on the same data and rules. Its deeper purpose is to turn Web3 event logs into a testbed for temporal intelligence: predicting user behavior transitions across long horizons while respecting censoring and non-stationarity.
wh: The hard part is that time-stamped transaction data is rich but not automatically understandable. A ledger records events, not intentions. If a user stops transacting, the record may not reveal whether the user churned, paused temporarily, moved elsewhere, or simply has not yet had enough time to show the next event. That is censoring: the outcome is partly hidden because observation ends before every story is complete. The second difficulty is non-stationarity, meaning the rules of the world do not stay fixed. A lending protocol, its users, market conditions, and platform usage can change across an extended horizon, so a pattern learned early may become less reliable later. A third difficulty is reproducibility. Without shared tasks, two groups can claim progress while using different data windows, labels, prediction horizons, and evaluation choices. The result is a field where methods cannot be compared cleanly and lessons from Web3 do not transfer well to broader web behavior modeling.
naive: A smart beginner would first sort each user's transactions by time, make simple counts such as number of deposits or recent activity, and train a generic prediction model to guess whether the user will remain active or transition to another state. That is a reasonable start because repeated behavior often says something about future behavior. It fails when the task is survival-like rather than ordinary classification. Users whose future is not fully observed cannot be treated as simple negative examples. It also fails when the platform changes over time: yesterday's easy rule may not hold months later. A second naive approach would compare papers by their reported scores, but that fails if each paper used a different dataset, time split, and definition of the event being predicted.
ap: The paper's central move is to make the evaluation problem itself concrete. Instead of proposing only another predictor, it presents the FinSurvival Challenge 2025 as a case study in how to benchmark temporal Web3 intelligence. The challenge uses 21.8 million Aave v3 transaction records and turns them into 16 survival prediction tasks. In plain terms, it asks systems to look at earlier user activity and predict later behavior transitions under shared rules. The key design choice is that the benchmark is meant to capture the two temporal problems named in the abstract: censoring and non-stationarity. It also reports lessons from winning solutions. The important finding is not just that a model can be trained on blockchain transactions, but that domain-aware temporal feature construction significantly outperformed generic modeling approaches. The paper therefore argues for benchmarks where the timeline, user-state definitions, and protocol-specific behavior are part of the task rather than incidental preprocessing.
mech: The mechanism begins with raw Aave v3 transaction records. Each record is an event fixed in time, and the full collection gives a longitudinal history of how users interact with the protocol. The benchmark first has to turn that event stream into prediction examples. That means choosing observation windows, defining which user behavior transition is being predicted, and deciding how far into the future the prediction should look. Because the abstract says there are 16 survival prediction tasks, the same transaction history is likely reorganized into several related questions about whether and when users move from one behavior state to another. The next step is handling incomplete futures. If a user has not shown the event by the end of observation, the benchmark should not automatically say the event will never happen; it records that the user was observed only up to a certain point. That is the censoring issue. Then participating methods build signals from the past. Generic methods may consume broad time-series summaries, while winning solutions apparently constructed temporal features that understand the domain, such as how the timing and sequence of protocol actions indicate user state. The benchmark compares submitted predictions under a common design, so the output is both task performance and a set of lessons about which kinds of temporal evidence matter in Web3 behavior prediction.
math: The main mathematical idea is survival prediction. Ordinary prediction asks, "will this label be true?" Survival prediction asks a more time-aware question: "how long until this event or transition happens, given what we have observed so far?" It exists because some users have not yet reached the event when the dataset ends. Treating all of them as event-free would confuse unknown future with known safety. The second idea is probability under partial observation. The system estimates chances of later behavior from repeated user histories, while keeping in mind that some histories are unfinished. The third idea is temporal feature construction. A feature is a measured clue; a temporal feature is a clue whose meaning depends on order, spacing, recency, or duration. In this paper, the abstract says domain-aware temporal features beat generic approaches, which means the useful clues were not just counts but measurements shaped by how Aave v3 behavior unfolds. The fourth idea is non-stationarity, the mathematical warning that data from one period may not be drawn from the same behavior pattern as data from another. The tradeoff is stable comparison versus real-world messiness: a benchmark must standardize the task enough to be fair while preserving the changing, censored timeline that makes the real problem hard.
dots: This paper sits in the temporal prediction part of the repository, near time-series and probability papers that ask how to act when evidence arrives over time and the future is only partly visible. It connects to churn prediction because one target is whether users continue or stop behaving in a system. It connects to risk modeling because Web3 financial actions are not just clicks; they can signal exposure and changing user states. It also connects to benchmark papers across the conference: the object being contributed is partly a shared measurement instrument, not only a new model. The repo's probability concept is relevant because the paper is estimating uncertain transitions from repeated cases. The sequence idea is relevant because event order and timing matter. The broader lesson for web analytics is that decentralized platforms offer unusually faithful event histories, but those histories still require careful task design before they can teach reliable lessons.
ww: The benchmark should help because it makes researchers confront the actual shape of the temporal problem instead of hiding it behind a convenient label. If every method must predict on the same Aave v3 histories, with the same survival tasks and the same treatment of time, then differences in results are more likely to reflect useful modeling choices rather than private dataset choices. Censoring matters because it prevents a common false lesson: that a user who has not yet transitioned is the same as a user who never will. Non-stationarity matters because a method that memorizes an early period can look strong until the platform or user population changes. Domain-aware temporal features work for an intuitive reason: user actions in a lending protocol have meanings tied to the protocol's mechanics and timing. The sequence, spacing, and type of actions can reveal a behavior state better than a generic model that sees only abstract event counts. The paper's case-study design turns that intuition into a reproducible comparison.
po: The payoff is a stronger foundation for studying temporal Web3 intelligence. The paper gives the field a concrete case study built from 21.8 million Aave v3 transactions and 16 survival prediction tasks, so future methods can be judged against shared temporal challenges rather than isolated private setups. It also reports a practical lesson: domain-aware temporal feature construction significantly outperformed generic modeling approaches. That matters beyond Web3 because churn, risk, and behavioral evolution appear throughout the wider web. Web3 supplies a high-fidelity event stream where those temporal problems can be studied with unusual detail.
limits: The claims depend on the benchmark design matching meaningful user behavior transitions, not merely convenient labels extracted from transaction logs. Aave v3 is one protocol, so lessons may not automatically transfer to other Web3 systems or ordinary web platforms. Domain-aware features can win because they capture real protocol structure, but they can also become too tied to one protocol or time period. The abstract does not specify the exact 16 tasks, evaluation measures, time splits, or winning methods, so the output can explain the benchmark logic but cannot verify every design choice. It also does not prove that Web3 is always a faithful sandbox for broader web dynamics.
